claim: Nanobodies are single-domain antibodies of camelid origin.
source: Nanobodies are single-domain antibodies of camelid origin.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about nanobodies, supported by the citation context in the introduction.

claim: Nanobodies are typically selected by phage display from an immune library.
source: Nanobodies represent antigen-binding domains of 'heavy-chain-only' camelid antibodies and are typically selected by phage display from an immune library (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993; Arbabi Ghahroudi et al., 1997; Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Nanobodies have a small size of approximately 13 kDa.
source: Their small size (~13 kDa), monoclonal nature and high specificity are ideal for applications like affinity purification or protein detection and localization (Helma et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated directly in the text with citation support.

claim: Nanobodies are commonly expressed in Escherichia coli and secreted into the oxidative periplasm.
source: Nanobodies are commonly expressed in Escherichia coli and secreted into the oxidative periplasm, where their conserved internal disulfide bond can be formed (Vincke et al., 2012; Pardon et al., 2014; Fridy et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations describing standard nanobody expression methods.

claim: Periplasmic expression of nanobodies often results in low final yield.
source: For example, it often results in low final yield (Baneyx and Mujacic, 2004), probably due to saturation of the secretion machinery and aggregation of precursor proteins in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by citation and includes speculative reasoning about the mechanism.

claim: The authors generated nanobodies against constituents of the Xenopus NPC scaffold, including Nup85, Nup93, Nup155, Nup98, and the Nup62•Nup58•Nup54 complex.
source: In order to provide new tools for studying NPCs, we generated nanobodies against constituents of the Xenopus NPC scaffold, namely Nup85, Nup93, and Nup155, as well as against Nup98 and the Nup62•Nup58•Nup54 complex.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental work performed by the authors.

claim: High-affinity nanobodies against all NPC targets were readily obtained from alpaca immune libraries by phage display.
source: High-affinity nanobodies against all these targets were readily obtained from alpaca immune libraries by phage display.
evidence: This describes the experimental outcome of the authors' work.

claim: Anti-NPC nanobodies could be produced in the cytoplasm of various E. coli strains.
source: We noticed that these nanobodies could be produced in the cytoplasm of various E. coli strains, as recently reported for other nanobodies (Olichon and Surrey, 2007; Zarschler et al., 2013; Djender et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments, supported by citations to similar findings.

claim: Fusing nanobodies behind a His14-bdNEDD8 module increased their yield dramatically.
source: We also observed that fusing nanobodies behind a His14-bdNEDD8 module (Frey and Görlich, 2014) increased their yield dramatically (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and cited methodology.

claim: Periplasmic secretion resulted in fully oxidized nanobodies.
source: While periplasmic secretion resulted in fully oxidized nanobodies, only a fraction of the SHuffle-expressed nanobodies contained a disulfide bond.
evidence: This is based on the maleimide shift assay results described in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Cytoplasmic expression in E. coli BLR yielded completely reduced nanobodies.
source: Cytoplasmic expression in E. coli BLR yielded completely reduced nanobodies.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from the maleimide shift assay.

claim: There was no affinity difference between reduced and disulfide bond-containing anti-Nup98 nanobodies.
source: A competition for antigen-binding revealed, however, no affinity difference between reduced and disulfide bond-containing anti-Nup98 nanobodies (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on experimental competition binding assay data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Reduced anti-Nup98 and anti-Nup93 nanobodies showed decreased thermostability compared to oxidized versions.
source: As expected, we observed by differential scanning fluorimetry (Niesen et al., 2007) a decreased thermostability of fully reduced anti-Nup98 and anti-Nup93 nanobodies (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on differential scanning fluorimetry data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The melting temperatures of reduced anti-Nup98 and anti-Nup93 nanobodies were 47°C and 57°C, respectively.
source: Their melting temperatures of 47°C and 57°C are, however, still well above any reasonable incubation temperature for downstream applications.
evidence: This is based on the differential scanning fluorimetry data.

claim: All nanobodies obtained via phage display against a wide range of antigens could be functionally produced in the E. coli cytoplasm.
source: All nanobodies that we obtained via phage display against a wide range of antigens could be functionally produced in the E. coli cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the authors' experimental observations across multiple nanobodies.

claim: The yield of cytoplasmic nanobody expression often exceeds 100 mg per liter of culture.
source: First, the yield often exceeds 100 mg per liter of culture and can be up to 30 times higher as compared to periplasmic expression (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on experimental yield measurements shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Cytoplasmic nanobody expression can yield up to 30 times higher than periplasmic expression.
source: First, the yield often exceeds 100 mg per liter of culture and can be up to 30 times higher as compared to periplasmic expression (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on comparative yield data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The anti-Nup85 nanobody retrieved the approximately 750 kDa nine-membered Y-complex as well as Tpr and Elys as specific but sub-stoichiometric binding partners.
source: The anti-Nup85 nanobody retrieved the ≈750 kDa nine-membered Y-complex as well as Tpr and Elys as specific but sub-stoichiometric binding partners.
evidence: This is based on the purification results shown in Figure 2b and mass spectrometry identification.

claim: For each nucleoporin complex, the authors achieved approximately 10,000-fold enrichment within a single native purification step.
source: For each complex we achieved a ≈10 000-fold enrichment within a single native purification step and yields of around 50%.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the purification results.

claim: The authors obtained 50-100 µg of Y-complex from 2 ml egg extract.
source: We obtained substantial amounts of the complex, namely 50–100 µg from as little as 2 ml egg extract, which initially contained ≈150 µg or ≈100 nM of the complex (Wühr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements of purified material with citation for initial concentration.

claim: The crystal structure of the anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 in complex with the globular Nup98 NPC anchor domain was solved at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: In order to better guide cysteine placement in the nanobody framework, we solved the crystal structure of the anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 in complex with the globular Nup98 NPC anchor domain (residues 716–866) at 1.9 Å resolution (Figure 5a, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data presented in Figure 5a and Table 1.

claim: TP377 contacts its target through all three CDR loops.
source: TP377 contacts its target through all three CDR loops and does not block the absolute Nup98 C-terminus, which anchors Nup98 via Nup96 or Nup88 to the NPC scaffold (Hodel et al., 2002; Griffis et al., 2003; Stuwe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure with citations for functional context.

claim: The internal disulfide bond-forming cysteines Cys22 and Cys96 of TP377 are reduced in the crystal structure.
source: The internal disulfide bond-forming cysteines Cys22 and Cys96 of TP377 are reduced in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure analysis.

claim: All individual cysteine mutants and nanobodies with up to three ectopic surface cysteines were well expressed and highly soluble in E. coli.
source: We found that not only all individual mutants, but also nanobodies with up to three ectopic surface cysteines were well expressed and highly soluble in E. coli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on expression and purification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Cysteines on all six positions on the anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 could be quantitatively labeled with maleimide fluorescent dyes.
source: Moreover, cysteines on all six positions on our model anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 could be quantitatively labeled with maleimide fluorescent dyes (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on labeling experiments shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The introduction of ectopic cysteines and their modification did not impair binding to the Nup98 target.
source: Importantly, competitive binding assays indicated that the introduction of ectopic cysteines and their modification did not impair binding to the Nup98 target (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Fluorophores attached via an N-terminal cysteine or A75C to anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 can be as close as approximately 2 nm to the target Nup98.
source: Based on the crystal structure, we estimate that fluorophores attached via an N-terminal cysteine or A75C to anti-Nup98 nanobody TP377 can be as close as ~2 nm to the target Nup98.
evidence: This is an estimate based on analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: All anti-Nup nanobody variants with Alexa Fluor 647 at different positions produced very bright punctuate nuclear rim staining characteristic for NPCs against very low background.
source: In confocal laser scanning microscopy, all variants produced a very bright punctuate nuclear rim staining of XL177 cells, characteristic for NPCs, against a very low background.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The Alexa Fluor 647 NHS-labeled anti-GFP nanobody Enhancer produced strong nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic background staining.
source: In contrast, when this nanobody was labeled at lysines with Alexa Fluor 647 NHS ester, it produced strong nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic background staining, which essentially obscured the specific signal.
evidence: This is based on comparative imaging data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The Alexa Fluor 647 maleimide-labeled anti-GFP nanobody Enhancer produced brilliant NPC signal with extremely low background.
source: When a HeLa Nup153-GFP cell line was stained, we observed a brilliant NPC signal for the Alexa Fluor 647 maleimide-labeled 'Enhancer', which perfectly coincided with the (weaker) GFP signal, and an extremely low background (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Singly Alexa Fluor 647 maleimide-labeled anti-Nup nanobodies were sufficient to produce enough localizations to reconstruct very detailed views of individual NPCs in STORM imaging.
source: Interestingly, singly Alexa Fluor 647 maleimide-labeled anti-Nup nanobodies were sufficient to produce enough localizations to reconstruct very detailed views of individual NPCs, where multiple copies of the imaged target proteins (Nup98, Nup93, and Nup155) appear arranged around the central NPC channel (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is based on STORM imaging data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Combining the N-terminal cysteine on the nanobody with the heterobifunctional crosslinker produced very prominent nanobody•Nup93 crosslinks.
source: However, combining the N-terminal cysteine on the nanobody with the (far shorter) heterobifunctional crosslinker, produced very prominent nanobody•Nup93 crosslinks.
evidence: This is based on crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 8a.

claim: TP179 binds to the middle region of the J-shaped structure of Nup93 surrounding residues K607 and K612.
source: TP179 binds to the middle region of the J-shaped structure of Nup93 surrounding residues K607 and K612 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a–b), while TP324 has a C-terminal epitope surrounding lysines K762, K765, and K782 of Nup93 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is based on crosslinking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: TP324 has a C-terminal epitope surrounding lysines K762, K765, and K782 of Nup93.
source: TP179 binds to the middle region of the J-shaped structure of Nup93 surrounding residues K607 and K612 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a–b), while TP324 has a C-terminal epitope surrounding lysines K762, K765, and K782 of Nup93 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is based on crosslinking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anti-Nup93 nanobody TP324 does not stain intact NPCs.
source: Accordingly, anti-Nup93 nanobody TP324 that targets the C-terminus of Nup93 does not stain intact NPCs (data not shown), but rather represents a good candidate to selectively disrupt NPC assembly.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation with speculative interpretation about its potential use.

claim: The C-terminal region of Nup93 is essential for NPC assembly.
source: The C-terminal region of Nup93 was previously shown to be essential for NPC assembly (Sachdev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Nanobody-purified endogenous Nup93 complexes analyzed by negative stain electron microscopy revealed characteristically curved α-solenoid fold-like particles.
source: Class averaging revealed characteristically curved α-solenoid fold-like particles, which are known to exhibit conformational flexibility (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data and class averaging shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The obtained Nup93 complex structures were reminiscent of the hook and eye-shaped structures reported for Nup188 and Nup205 orthologues from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Myceliophthora thermophila.
source: The obtained structures were very reminiscent of the hook and eye-shaped structures reported earlier for the Nup188 and Nup205 orthologues from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Amlacher et al., 2011) and Myceliophthora thermophila (Andersen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the authors' EM data with previously published structures.

claim: The overall shape of the Nup93 complexes is conserved from fungi to vertebrates.
source: This suggests not only that the overall shape of the Nup93 complexes is conserved from fungi to vertebrates, but also that our single-step purification strategy for large protein complexes yields material of sufficient quality for a direct structural analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity observed in the EM data.

claim: The single-step purification strategy yields material of sufficient quality for direct structural analysis.
source: This suggests not only that the overall shape of the Nup93 complexes is conserved from fungi to vertebrates, but also that our single-step purification strategy for large protein complexes yields material of sufficient quality for a direct structural analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quality of the EM data obtained from nanobody-purified complexes.

claim: At 0°C, scaffold cysteines of nanobodies remained fully protected from maleimide modification in native buffer.
source: Importantly, they remained fully protected at 0°C, predicting that maleimide-labeling on ice would be fully selective for engineered surface cysteines.
evidence: This is based on the biotin-maleimide modification experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Scaffold cysteines became modified at 37°C in native buffer, pointing to transient exposure through thermal breathing.
source: After unfolding by urea, the scaffold cysteines became modified at either 37°C, 23°C, or 0°C. In native buffer, however, modification was quantitative only at 37°C, pointing to a transient exposure of the otherwise buried scaffold cysteines ('thermal breathing').
evidence: This is based on the biotin-maleimide modification experiments shown in Figure 4 with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Modification of framework lysines likely creates hydrophobic patches that favor unspecific binding and aggregation.
source: This comparison indicated that modification of (multiple) framework lysines likely creates hydrophobic patches that favor unspecific binding and aggregation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the comparative imaging data showing high background with NHS-labeled nanobodies.

claim: NPCs have a diameter well below the diffraction limit.
source: Due to a diameter well below the diffraction limit, NPCs have been studied by super-resolution microscopy using either indirect immunofluorescence (Löschberger et al., 2012; Göttfert et al., 2013) or the anti-GFP nanobody (Szymborska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPCs supported by citations to super-resolution microscopy studies.

claim: The NPC has a very large size of approximately 110 MDa.
source: Their very large size of ≈110 MDa not only places them amongst the largest molecular machines, but also poses formidable challenges for any structural and functional investigation (reviewed in Hurt and Beck, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPCs supported by a review citation.

claim: The Nup107-Nup160 or Y-shaped complex is the most characteristic NPC subcomplex.
source: Certainly, the most characteristic subcomplex is the Nup107-Nup160 or Y-shaped complex (Siniossoglou et al., 2000; Vasu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC structure supported by citations.

claim: The Y-shaped complex has an essential role in NPC assembly.
source: Its essential role in NPC assembly (Harel et al., 2003; Walther et al., 2003) as well as its structural organization and relative position within the NPC have been studied intensely (Bui et al., 2013; Eibauer et al., 2015; Kelley et al., 2015; Stuwe et al., 2015b; von Appen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: FG-repeat domains of Nup98 and the Nup62 complex form a permeability barrier within the central NPC channel.
source: We also purified the Nup98•Gle2 and the Nup62•Nup58•Nup54 complex using anti-Nup98 and anti-Nup54 nanobodies, respectively. Here, we included a RanQ69L•GTP wash to release nuclear transport receptors, which otherwise would remain bound to the FG domains of Nup98 or the Nup62 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC function, with experimental data showing the need for RanQ69L•GTP wash.

claim: Two alpacas were immunized with 0.5-1.0 mg protein or protein complex at 3-4 week intervals for 3-4 times.
source: Two female alpacas, held at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry, were immunized with 0.5–1.0 mg protein or protein complex at 3–4 week intervals for 3–4 times.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental immunization protocol.

claim: A library of 2-3 x 10^8 individual transformants was generated for nanobody selection.
source: A library of 2–3 x 108 individual transformants was infected with helper phage M13KO7 (New England Biolabs) and VHH-displaying bacteriophages were produced overnight while shaking at 37°C.
evidence: This is a description of the phage display library size.

claim: Typically three rounds of panning with decreasing antigen concentration were performed.
source: Typically three rounds of panning with decreasing antigen concentration (e.g. 100 nM, 20 nM, and 1 nM) and increasingly thorough washing were performed.
evidence: This is a description of the phage display selection protocol.

claim: The crystal structure belongs to space group P41.
source: Crystals belonged to the space group P41 and diffracted to 1.9 Å (see Table 1).
evidence: This is crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Molecular replacement was performed using a published nanobody structure (PDB 4KRN) as a search model.
source: For structure determination, molecular replacement was performed in PHASER with a published nanobody structure (PDB 4KRN; Schmitz et al., 2013) as a search model.
evidence: This describes the crystallographic method with citation to the search model.

claim: In traditional indirect immunofluorescence, the effective displacement between label and epitope can reach up to 24-30 nm.
source: In traditional indirect immunofluorescence, epitopes are initially decorated with a primary antibody and detected with a fluorophore-labeled secondary one, each around 12–15 nm in size (Harris et al., 1998). The effective displacement between label and epitope can reach up to 24–30 nm and thus significantly deteriorate the achievable precision and accuracy of protein localization by super-resolution fluorescence microscopy (Hell, 2009; Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about immunofluorescence limitations supported by citations.

claim: Nanobodies have a diameter of 4 nm.
source: Nanobodies (diameter: 4 nm) are an ideal solution to this problem (Ries et al., 2012; Szymborska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nanobody size supported by citations.

claim: NHS ester labeling of nanobodies at lysines is random and rarely quantitative.
source: So far, nanobodies were labeled at lysines by N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) ester fluorophores (Ries et al., 2012; Fridy et al., 2014), which is random and rarely quantitative.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing labeling methods supported by citations.

claim: NHS ester labeling deteriorates signal-to-background ratios or even completely abolishes epitope recognition.
source: As we show below, it also deteriorates signal-to-background ratios or even completely abolishes epitope recognition.
evidence: This is a forward reference to experimental results shown later in the manuscript.

claim: Adding an extra C-terminal cysteine to a periplasmically expressed nanobody led to severe reduction in yield and caused extensive dimerization.
source: Adding an extra C-terminal cysteine (for subsequent maleimide modification) to a periplasmically expressed nanobody was also not a satisfying solution, because it led to a severe reduction in yield and caused extensive dimerization (Massa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of problems with previous approaches supported by citation.

claim: The anti-Nup93 nanobody TP179 contains a lysine in CDR II and lost antigen-binding after NHS modification.
source: The anti-Nup93 nanobody TP179 contains a lysine in CDR II and even lost antigen-binding after NHS modification.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the effect of NHS labeling on a specific nanobody.

claim: Maleimide-labeling of exposed cysteines is quantitative even with just stoichiometric amounts of labeling reagent.
source: In contrast, maleimide-labeling of exposed cysteines is quantitative even with just stoichiometric amounts of labeling reagent and thus far more economical.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental observations with maleimide labeling.

claim: NHS esters react not only with amino groups but also rapidly hydrolyze in aqueous buffers.
source: NHS esters have the additional disadvantage that they react not only with amino groups, but also rapidly hydrolyze in aqueous buffers.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about NHS ester reactivity.

claim: The NPC has become a benchmark for many new advancements of super-resolution microscopy.
source: Because of its well-defined dimension and symmetric structure, the NPC has become a benchmark for many new advancements of super-resolution microscopy (Schermelleh et al., 2008; Szymborska et al., 2013; Göttfert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the use of NPCs in microscopy supported by citations.
